content: The findings from 10 studies (references 111-120) were reviewed to evaluate treatment outcomes when antiretroviral therapy (ART) and second-line tuberculosis (TB) drugs were used concurrently. None of the data originated from randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Individual participant data were available for 217 individuals with drug-resistant TB, of whom 127 received ART. The quality of evidence from individual observational studies ranged from low to very low certainty. Pooled data from longitudinal cohort studies indicated that individuals receiving ART had a lower risk of death and a higher likelihood of cure and resolution of TB symptoms compared to those not receiving ART, although the evidence was of low quality. Evidence for other critical outcomes, such as severe adverse effects from second-line TB drugs, sputum smear or culture conversion, drug interactions between ART and TB medications, and treatment default rates, was of very low quality. Additionally, the available data did not allow for assessment of other important outcomes, such as preventing additional drug resistance, reducing TB transmission, achieving relapse-free cure, determining the optimal duration of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) treatment, avoiding unnecessary MDR-TB treatment, reducing costs, and improving access to appropriate care. Recommendation 30: Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis for people living with HIV and diagnosed TB Co-trimoxazole, a fixed-dose combination of sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim, is an antimicrobial agent that prevents a range of secondary bacterial, fungal, and protozoan infections. It is recommended for all people living with HIV who also have TB, regardless of their CD4 count. Evidence from RCTs, including in areas with high antibiotic resistance, has demonstrated reduced mortality, morbidity, and hospitalization without a significant increase in adverse events among people living with HIV and smear-positive TB, irrespective of CD4 counts (references 121, 122). Non-randomized and operational studies also showed that co-trimoxazole preventive therapy is feasible, safe, and reduces mortality rates in people with TB (references 123, 125). Recommendation 31: ART initiation in TB treatment settings and linkages to HIV care Coordination between TB and HIV programs is essential to deliver comprehensive and uninterrupted care for individuals with both conditions. This approach can also reduce out-of-pocket costs associated with traveling to multiple appointments (reference 126). Community engagement, patient education, adherence counseling, and peer support are critical for early recognition of adverse events, retention in care, and adherence to co-treatment. A systematic review of 19 observational studies found that delivering ART in TB treatment settings increased ART uptake and timeliness of initiation, although data on mortality and TB treatment success were inconsistent. Similarly, five studies evaluating TB treatment in HIV care settings reported decreased or comparable mortality rates and similar TB treatment success and ART uptake across studies. HIV Prevention and Collaborative TB/HIV Services TB programs should implement comprehensive HIV prevention strategies for individuals attending TB care and their partners, targeting sexual, parenteral, or vertical transmission. Personnel working with individuals with presumptive or diagnosed TB, people living with HIV, and people who use drugs should assess HIV risk factors and provide comprehensive information and services to minimize risks. HIV Prevention Interventions for People with TB The WHO recommends combination HIV prevention programs that use evidence-based biomedical, behavioral, and structural interventions tailored to local HIV epidemiology and context. These approaches are relevant for people with TB and their contacts who are at risk of or living with HIV. Behavioral interventions include targeted education on HIV prevention, while structural interventions address barriers to accessing services by reducing stigma, promoting gender equality, and supporting economic and social empowerment. Preventing HIV transmission in healthcare settings requires standard precautions, injection safety, blood safety, and safe waste disposal, as well as occupational PEP following needle-stick injuries. Monitoring and Evaluation of Collaborative TB/HIV Activities Monitoring and evaluation are critical to assess the quality, effectiveness, and coverage of collaborative TB/HIV activities. Electronic health records and unique identifiers can enhance data collection and analysis while minimizing duplication. National TB/HIV coordination mechanisms play a vital role in coordinating monitoring and evaluation and convening stakeholders for regular reviews. These reviews should include data analysis, adjustments to service delivery, and tracking the impact of these adjustments. Research Gaps in HIV-Associated TB Several research gaps were identified, including the need for well-designed clinical trials to evaluate TB screening and diagnostic algorithms, the effectiveness of ART initiation among people with TB symptoms, and the role of prophylactic corticosteroids in reducing immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). Additional studies are needed to optimize TB treatment regimens, including shorter and better-tolerated preventive treatments, and to evaluate the safety and efficacy of newer drugs and regimens for drug-resistant TB. Research on integrating TB and HIV services, improving adherence to treatment, and addressing the needs of specific populations, such as children, pregnant women, and people with comorbidities, is also a priority.
